summary: The Northern Alps of central Honshu, across four prefectures: peaks over 3,000 metres, glacial cirques that hold snow through summer, active volcanoes and the first glaciers confirmed in Japan. Walk the Azusa valley at Kamikochi, ride the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route up to Murodo, or take a bus to 2,702 metres on Norikura. One of Japan's first national parks, designated in 1934.
story: The Hida Mountains (飛騨山脈), the Northern Alps, were pushed up along a great fault on their eastern side and have been cut down by water and ice ever since. From the middle of the park the Kurobe flows north, the Azusa south, the Takase east and the Gamata west, each in a deep V-shaped valley. Higher up, glaciers of colder times scooped the cirques of Karasawa, Yakushi and Tateyama. Snow still lies all summer in the great snow gullies of Tsurugisawa, Hakuba and Harinoki, and in 2012 three snowfields on Tateyama and Tsurugi, holding ice around 30 metres thick that slowly flows, were recognised as the first active glaciers confirmed in Japan.

Volcanoes complicate the picture. Yakedake (焼岳), still active, erupted in 1915 and dammed the Azusa River, making the pond of Taishō-ike at the mouth of Kamikochi. Around Tateyama, the fumaroles of Jigokudani, the crater lakes at Murodo and the lava plateau of Midagahara come from the same kind of fire. Plants step up with the altitude: beech and Mongolian oak below about 1,500 metres, Veitch's and Maries' fir and Erman's birch to about 2,500, then creeping pine and flower meadows. Rock ptarmigan (雷鳥 raichō), a bird left behind by the ice age, lives up there with stoats and alpine butterflies; Asiatic black bears, serow and macaques live lower down.

Tateyama (立山) was a holy mountain long before it was a climb. With Fuji and Hakusan it is counted among Japan's three sacred peaks, and Edo-period pilgrims saw the steaming valley of Jigokudani, below the summit, as hell, so the climb to the summit took them from the underworld to heaven. The priest Banryū (播隆) reached the top of Yarigatake in 1828. The English engineer and archaeologist William Gowland, who climbed it in 1878, called the range the Japanese Alps, and the missionary Walter Weston's 1896 book carried the name abroad. A memorial to Weston stands at Kamikochi.

The park was designated on 4 December 1934, in the same group as Akan, Daisetsuzan, Nikko and Aso, among Japan's first national parks. Roads came later, and so did limits on them. The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route, open throughout since 1971, crosses the Tateyama range by cable car, bus, ropeway and electric bus, and private cars are kept off its Toyama-side road. Kamikochi closed its road to private cars in summer from 1975 and all year from 1996, and the Norikura Skyline followed in 2003. Most visitors now reach the high country by public transport.
howItWorks: Like every Japanese national park, Chubusangaku is a zoned regional park rather than a fenced reserve. The Ministry of the Environment sets the rules, but people live, work and do business inside it. Here the state holds most of the land, about 155,000 of the park's 174,323 hectares, and the rest is public or private: the hotels and campsites of Kamikochi, hot-spring inns, mountain huts on the ridges, the Alpine Route and the Kurobe Dam. The park spans Niigata, Toyama, Nagano and Gifu prefectures and fourteen cities, towns and villages.

More than a third of the park, about 64,000 hectares, is special protection zone (特別保護地区), the strictest category, where picking any plant, taking a stone or lighting a fire needs a permit. A further 87,000 hectares are special zones (特別地域) of three grades, where building, felling and collecting listed plants need permission, and about 23,000 hectares are ordinary zone, where only larger works must be notified. For a walker the rule is the same everywhere: stay on the path, take nothing and camp only at the designated sites. In the Tsugaike area of Otari, beside Hakuba, snowmobiles and other vehicles are barred from 348 hectares of the special zone.

Other designations overlap the park. Kamikochi is also a Special Place of Scenic Beauty and a Special Natural Monument under the cultural-properties law, and keeps its own five rules for visitors. Since 2012 the wetlands of Midagahara and Dainichidaira on Tateyama, 574 hectares, have been a Ramsar site, which the Ministry describes as the highest-lying in Japan. Access is managed as much as land: Kamikochi, Norikura and the Toyama side of the Alpine Route are closed to private cars, and visitors change to buses or taxis at car parks below.

sights.name: Kamikochi and Kappa-bashi (上高地・河童橋)
sights.note: A level valley floor at about 1,500 metres on the Azusa River, where the suspension bridge looks up to the Hotaka peaks. Reached only by bus or taxi.

sights.name: Murodō and Mikurigaike (室堂・みくりが池)
sights.note: The Alpine Route's highest stop at 2,450 metres, beside a blue crater lake, with paths up Oyama and towards the fumaroles of Jigokudani.

sights.name: Yarigatake (槍ヶ岳)
sights.note: The spear-shaped 3,180-metre summit at the head of the Azusa, first climbed by the priest Banryū in 1828.

sights.name: Karasawa cirque and the Hotaka peaks (涸沢・穂高連峰)
sights.note: A glacial cirque under Okuhotakadake, at 3,190 metres the joint third-highest mountain in Japan. Famous for autumn colour.

sights.name: Taishō-ike (大正池)
sights.note: The pond made in 1915 when an eruption of Yakedake dammed the Azusa River; the volcano, still active, rises behind it.

sights.name: Mount Norikura (乗鞍岳)
sights.note: The park's southern volcano. Buses climb to Tatamidaira at 2,702 metres, among alpine flowers below the 3,026-metre summit, Kengamine.

sights.name: Hakuba Daisekkei (白馬大雪渓)
sights.note: One of Japan's three great snow gullies, climbed on snow on the way up Shiroumadake (2,932 metres).

sights.name: Shōmyō Falls (称名滝)
sights.note: Japan's highest waterfall: 350 metres in four drops off the edge of the Midagahara plateau.

sights.name: Kamikochi Visitor Center
sights.note: The Ministry of the Environment's centre near Kappa-bashi: trail conditions, bear sightings, nature walks. Open late April to 15 November.

sights.name: Kamikochi Information Centre
sights.note: At the Kamikochi bus terminal: maps, weather and transport information. Open late April to 15 November.

sights.name: Tateyama Nature Conservation Centre
sights.note: Toyama Prefecture's centre at Murodō on the area's nature. Open mid-April to mid-November.

sights.name: Keyakidaira Visitor Center
sights.note: At the end of the Kurobe Gorge Railway, with trail conditions and films on the gorge. Open while the railway runs.

entrances: Kamikochi, by shuttle bus or taxi from Sawando car park on the Nagano side, where the Sawando National Park Gate gives information, or from Hirayu Akandana car park on the Gifu side
Tateyama Station (Toyama) and Ōgizawa (Nagano), the two ends of the Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route
Unazuki Onsen, for the Kurobe Gorge Railway up the Kurobe valley to Keyakidaira
The Hakuba valley, with cable cars up to Tsugaike Nature Park and Happo-one
Hirayu Onsen and Hoonokidaira (Gifu) and Norikura Kōgen (Nagano), for buses up Norikura; the Shin-Hotaka Ropeway from Okuhida
planYourVisit.reservations: No permit or entry booking is needed for the park itself. Alpine Route tickets can be bought online with a boarding time reserved, and the snow-wall season and Japanese holidays are the busiest. Mountain huts expect guests to book, and most open only between late spring and early November; Nagano Prefecture's mountain-hut portal lists each hut's dates and booking rules. Shuttle-bus timetables, road openings and hut seasons change every year: check with the operators before you go.
permits: Climbing plan (登山計画書): required by Nagano Prefecture on its designated trails and by Gifu Prefecture in its Northern Alps and active-volcano areas; file it before you set out
Winter climbs in the Tsurugi area: Toyama Prefecture requires a climbing notice in advance
Drones: contact the landowner or manager before flying anywhere in the park; flying is not allowed at Kamikochi
camping: Konashidaira Campground, five minutes' walk from Kappa-bashi
Tokusawa Campground and Yokoo, further up the Azusa towards Yarigatake and Hotaka
Raichōzawa camp site, about 45 minutes' walk below Murodō
Tents are allowed only at designated sites
lodging: Hotels and inns at Kamikochi, open from late April to mid-November
Hot-spring inns at Hirayu, Shirahone, Nakanoyu and Sawando
Hotels and lodges along the Alpine Route, including at Murodō
Mountain huts on the main ridges and in the high valleys, booked in advance
seasonalClosures: The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route closes for the winter; in 2026 it ran from 15 April to 30 November
The road into Kamikochi closes from 16 November to mid-April, and the shuttles, hotels and visitor centres close with it
The Norikura Skyline is open from mid-May to 31 October, and the upper Echo Line is open to buses and taxis from July, with only spring buses before that; both close for the winter on 1 November
The Kurobe Gorge Railway runs from spring to late autumn; cut short by damage from the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake, it reopened to Keyakidaira on 1 October 2026

weather: This is heavy-snow country, and snow decides the year. The high roads open in April, when the Alpine Route runs between snow walls that can stand about 20 metres high near Murodō; snow lingers in the gullies right through summer. At Murodō, 2,450 metres up, the operator's monthly averages run from a high of 6°C and a low of −3°C in April to 18°C and 12°C in August, and back to 2°C and −5°C in November, about 15°C colder than sea level. Alpine flowers bloom at Tatamidaira from mid-July to mid-August. Autumn colour starts on the summits in mid-September and works down the valleys into early November, and by mid-November Kamikochi and the high roads are closing for the winter.
directions: For Kamikochi, take a JR Azusa limited express from Shinjuku to Matsumoto, the Alpico Kamikochi Line to Shin-Shimashima and a bus up the valley; from the Gifu side, take a Nohi Bus from Takayama to Hirayu Onsen and change there. Drivers leave their cars at Sawando or Hirayu Akandana and continue by shuttle bus or taxi; direct buses also run from Tokyo, Nagoya and Osaka. For the Alpine Route, take the Hokuriku Shinkansen to Toyama and the Toyama Chihō Railway to Tateyama Station, or start from the Nagano end with a bus from Shinano-Ōmachi (JR Ōito Line) or Nagano to Ōgizawa. The Kurobe Gorge Railway leaves from Unazuki Onsen, reached by Toyama Chihō Railway from Shin-Kurobe, next to Kurobe-Unazukionsen on the Hokuriku Shinkansen. Hakuba is on the JR Ōito Line and has buses from Nagano.

chronology.text: The priest Banryū makes the first recorded ascent of Yarigatake.
William Gowland climbs Yarigatake, the first foreigner known to do so; he later names the range the Japanese Alps.
Walter Weston publishes Mountaineering and Exploration in the Japanese Alps in London.
An eruption of Yakedake dams the Azusa River and forms Taishō-ike.
Chubusangaku is designated a national park on 4 December, with Akan, Daisetsuzan, Nikko and Aso.
The Tateyama Kurobe Alpine Route opens throughout, from Tateyama to Ōgizawa.
Private cars are kept off the Kamikochi road in July and August; the ban becomes year-round in 1996.
The Norikura Skyline closes to private cars.
Moving ice is confirmed in snowfields on Tateyama and Tsurugi, Japan's first known active glaciers; Midagahara and Dainichidaira become a Ramsar site.
The Kurobe Gorge Railway runs to Keyakidaira again for the first time since the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake.

safety: Asiatic black bears live throughout the park, including the floor of Kamikochi. Make noise as you walk, never leave food or rubbish out, and check recent sightings at a visitor centre; Kamikochi Visitor Centre posts them.

Yakedake, Norikura and Midagahara on Tateyama are active volcanoes under the Japan Meteorological Agency's five eruption alert levels: 1 'potential for increased activity', 2 'do not approach the crater', 3 'do not approach the volcano', 4 'elderly and vulnerable people evacuate' and 5 'evacuate'. Check the current level on the JMA website before you climb.

At Tateyama the path through Jigokudani is closed because of volcanic gas, and gas can build up on the nearby path between Enmadai and the Dainichi viewpoint depending on wind and weather. Do not stop or rest there.

Buses lift visitors to 2,450 metres at Murodō and 2,702 metres at Tatamidaira, and the ridges beyond pass 3,000 metres. Climb slowly and turn back with headache or nausea. Even in August Murodō averages only 12–18°C, so carry warm and waterproof layers.

Snow lies on the high routes into summer: the Hakuba Daisekkei is climbed on snow, and spring visitors to Murodō must follow its snow-season rules. The Daikiretto ridge between Hotaka and Yari is often called the hardest route in Japan that needs no climbing equipment.
regulations: Private cars may not drive into Kamikochi at any time of year, nor up the Norikura Skyline or the upper Echo Line, nor along the Alpine Route between Tateyama Station and Ōgizawa. Park at the transfer car parks and take a bus or taxi.
Kamikochi's rules: take nothing, feed nothing, bring no pets or non-native species, carry all rubbish home and stay on the paths. Bicycles are not allowed on footpaths and drones may not be flown.
Camp only at designated sites. Do not chase rock ptarmigan or step into the vegetation to photograph them.

In the special protection zone, picking plants, collecting stones and lighting fires are prohibited without a permit. In the Tsugaike area of Otari, beside Hakuba, snowmobiles and other vehicles are barred from the special zone.
